reviewer: Codex deut_7_10 (AI-assisted supplied-English curation for Judges17–21)
review_method: Read all147 complete actual source units, all complete retained targets and necessary immediate contexts. External readings included Genesis19:1–11/35:22–26, Exodus18:1–4/20:4–5, Deuteronomy12:8–14/17:2–7/22:25–27/27:15, Joshua8:4–8/15–22,15:63,18:1,19:40–48, Numbers25:10–13/27:18–23/31:7–18,1Samuel11:7–8 and1Chronicles12:1–2, plus Judges1:1–2,8:27,13:24–25 and all17–21. Then independently displayed and reread all151 complete source/target/relationship/rationale triples in five untruncated chapter files. Preserved the original draft, recorded exactly13 explanatory precision changes and separately displayed and reread all13 complete corrected triples before freezing. Local links identify particular question/answer, offer/response, plan/performance, property transfer, source framing, numbered-force repetition or stated casualty and oath constraints; they do not claim independent corroboration. Proposed conventional episode identity using Joshua19:48 was read but remains uncounted. This is initial supplied-English curation, not exhaustive discovery or original-language, apparatus, historical chronology, modern site identification or independent human specialist verification.
pin_method: Fresh raw fetch of all8 retained source books at the fixed commit. old_row.relationship: Household ephods in related accounts with different assessments
old_row.rationale: Micah's sanctuary contains an ephod and teraphim and has his son as priest; the earlier Gideon account expressly calls its ephod a stumbling block to Gideon and his household. The two ephods are not identified as one object.

new_row.relationship: Ephods and household consequences in related accounts
new_row.rationale: Micah's sanctuary contains an ephod and teraphim and has his son as priest; the earlier Gideon account expressly calls its ephod a stumbling block to Gideon and his household. The two ephods are not identified as one object.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter pleased response and departure follow the tribal offer
old_row.rationale: After the invitation to become the tribe's father and priest, the priest is glad, takes the listed objects and joins the people, narrating his response without declaring the choice righteous.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter pleased response and joining the people follow the tribal offer
new_row.rationale: After the invitation to become the tribe's father and priest, the priest is glad, takes the listed objects and joins the people, narrating his response without declaring the choice righteous.

old_row.relationship: Jebus-Jerusalem and the recorded Jebusite residence
old_row.rationale: The traveler reaches Jebus, expressly identified as Jerusalem; Joshua describes Jebusites living in Jerusalem whom Judah could not destroy. The related residence notice is retained without supplying an unrecorded conquest chronology.

new_row.relationship: Jebus-Jerusalem and the recorded Jebusite residence
new_row.rationale: The traveler comes opposite Jebus, expressly identified as Jerusalem; Joshua describes Jebusites living in Jerusalem whom Judah could not destroy. The related residence notice is retained without supplying an unrecorded conquest chronology.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter suggested Jebusite lodging rejected by the master
old_row.rationale: The servant proposes lodging in the Jebusite city because it is late; the master refuses a foreigner's city outside Israel and proposes Gibeah instead.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter suggested Jebusite lodging rejected by the master
new_row.rationale: The servant proposes lodging in the Jebusite city because it is late; the master refuses a foreigner's city that does not belong to the sons of Israel and proposes Gibeah instead.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter proposed Gibeah-or-Ramah lodging and arrival at Gibeah
old_row.rationale: The master offers Gibeah or Ramah as places to lodge; the journey then reaches Benjamin's Gibeah as the sun sets, identifying which proposed destination is reached.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter proposed Gibeah-or-Ramah lodging and approach to Gibeah
new_row.rationale: The master offers Gibeah or Ramah for lodging; the following notice places sunset near Benjamin's Gibeah, identifying the party's approach to one proposed destination.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter sunset arrival and unsuccessful initial search for lodging
old_row.rationale: The party passes to Gibeah at sunset and turns into that city to lodge, but its initial wait in the square brings no invitation into a house.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter sunset approach and unsuccessful initial lodging search
new_row.rationale: The party comes near Gibeah at sunset and then turns into that city to lodge; its initial wait in the square brings no invitation into a house.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter available provisions and the host's subsequent hospitality
old_row.rationale: The traveler says they have fodder, bread and wine and lack nothing; the old man nevertheless brings him inside, feeds the pack animals and shares washing, eating and drinking. No exhaustion of the travelers' provisions is asserted.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter available provisions and the host's subsequent hospitality
new_row.rationale: The traveler says they have fodder, bread and wine and lack nothing; the old man nevertheless brings him inside and supplies fodder, followed by washing, eating and drinking. No exhaustion of the travelers' provisions or additional meal participant is asserted.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter renewed unity formula recalls the initial assembly
old_row.rationale: The later gathering as one man repeats the initial congregation's as-one-man description at Mizpah, linking the city's assembled men with the narrated national mobilization.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter renewed unity formula recalls the initial assembly
new_row.rationale: The later gathering as one man repeats the initial congregation's as-one-man description at Mizpah, linking the men gathered from the cities with the narrated national mobilization.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter unrecognized disaster later expressly perceived by Benjamin
old_row.rationale: The earlier account says disaster had arrived without being known; the later account expressly names Benjamin seeing that disaster had reached them. The earlier unnamed pronoun is not independently assigned a new speaker.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter unrecognized disaster later expressly perceived by Benjamin
new_row.rationale: The earlier account says disaster had arrived without being known; the later account expressly names Benjamin seeing that disaster had reached them. The earlier unnamed pronoun is not independently assigned a new named subject.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter retrospective explanation of the deliberate giving of ground
old_row.rationale: The narrative explains that Israel gave ground because it trusted its ambush, corresponding to its earlier stated plan to flee and draw Benjamin out. The explanation is not treated as a genuine initial rout.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter retrospective explanation of the deliberate giving of ground
new_row.rationale: The narrative explains that Israel gave ground because it trusted its ambush, corresponding to its earlier plan to flee and draw Benjamin out. This concerns the deliberate third-day movement, preserving the earlier days' defeats.

old_row.relationship: Different campaigns distinguish women by the stated male-bed criterion
old_row.rationale: Both instructions name every male and women who have known a male's bed, while the following preservation concerns those who have not. The Midian campaign and Jabesh-gilead expedition, speakers and circumstances remain distinct.

new_row.relationship: Different campaigns distinguish women by the stated male-bed criterion
new_row.rationale: Both give the male-bed criterion for women; Judges says every male, while Numbers specifies males among the dependents. The next preserved females in each account have not known a male's bed. The campaigns and speakers remain distinct.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter four hundred recovered women are later given to Benjamin
old_row.rationale: The four hundred young virgins found at Jabesh-gilead are brought to Shiloh; the later account says Benjamin receives women from Jabesh-gilead and is pleased. No missing-wife figure or additional shortage clause is inserted.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter four hundred identified women are later given to Benjamin
new_row.rationale: The four hundred young virgins found at Jabesh-gilead are brought to Shiloh; the later account records giving women from Jabesh-gilead to Benjamin and says this pleased them. No missing-wife figure or specific referent for that final pronoun is supplied.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter declaration of preserved inheritance followed by resettlement
old_row.rationale: The people insist Benjamin's inheritance be preserved and the tribe not blotted out; the later account records return to that inheritance and rebuilding cities, alongside its report of wives being seized.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter declaration of preserved inheritance followed by resettlement
new_row.rationale: The people say an inheritance is preserved for Benjamin and the tribe shall not be blotted out; the later account records return to that inheritance and rebuilding cities, alongside its report of wives being seized.
